conceptTag: Pitch a decision to a skeptical CEO
readerTitle: Five minutes to win over a skeptical CEO
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (12개 매장 레스토랑 그룹의 자체 온라인 주문 시스템 도입 제안) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 회의적인 CEO는 '좋은 아이디어인가'보다 '이 사람에게 위험을 맡겨도 되는가'를 묻는다. 결론 먼저, 단점 먼저, 숫자 하나, 한 장 메모는 모두 그 질문에 대한 답이다.
misconception: 회의적인 상대는 더 많은 자료와 더 강한 확신으로 설득해야 한다.

sources.text: 모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 계산 확인: 배달앱 주문 매출 월 $200,000 × 수수료 25%(가정) = 월 $50,000. 이 중 30%($60,000)가 자체 채널로 옮기면 수수료 절감 $15,000 − 자체 채널 비용 5%(결제·마케팅 가정) $3,000 − 소프트웨어 월 $3,000 = 월 $9,000 절감.
시범 비용 $9,000 = 소프트웨어 월 $3,000 × 90일(3개월) 가정. 월 $9,000 절감은 그룹 전체 적용 시 추정치이며 시범 비용과 금액이 같은 것은 우연임. 독자 혼동 여부를 검토하세요.
배달앱 수수료율은 나라와 계약마다 크게 다르므로 카드 본문에는 구체적 비율을 쓰지 않고 금액만 제시했습니다.

cards.title: Five minutes to win over a skeptical CEO
body: You run operations for a group of 12 restaurants. Delivery apps now bring in a big share of orders, and they take a cut of every one. You want to launch your own online ordering.
The CEO has blocked two tech projects before. You get five minutes on Monday. Four moments will decide how it goes.

image.label: A manager waiting outside a CEO's office with a single sheet of paper
image.brief: 레스토랑 본사 사무실 복도. 운영 책임자가 종이 한 장을 들고 CEO 사무실 문 앞에 서 있고, 문 너머 CEO는 팔짱을 끼고 시계를 보는 실루엣. 벽시계에 '5분' 느낌. 실제 배달앱 로고나 브랜드는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The CEO looks at the clock and says, "Go."
body: You have five minutes and a listener who expects to say no. How do you open?

options.text: Explain how delivery apps grew and why their fees keep rising
options.feedback: Useful context, but the CEO spends three minutes wondering what you want. By the time you reach the ask, time and patience are gone.

options.text: "I recommend we test our own online ordering in three restaurants for 90 days. It costs $9,000. I need a yes today."
options.feedback: The CEO knows the ask in ten seconds and can spend the rest of the meeting testing it. You give up suspense, which you never needed.

options.text: "Have you seen what we paid delivery apps last month?"
options.feedback: It grabs attention, but a skeptic hears a setup. They brace for a sales pitch instead of listening to a proposal.

cards.title: "Our last app project went nowhere. Why is this different?"
body: Say you chose to lead with the answer. The CEO doesn't argue with the idea. They argue with the risk. What do you say?

options.text: Insist this vendor is far better and it won't happen again
options.feedback: It sounds confident, but you've promised something you can't prove. The CEO now trusts you less, not more.

options.text: Name the downsides yourself: some customers won't switch, staff need training, and we keep the delivery apps during the test
options.feedback: You show the costs before the CEO has to dig for them. Admitting what you give up makes the upside easier to believe.

options.text: Agree the risk is real and promise a full report later
options.feedback: Respectful, but vague. The CEO still doesn't know what could go wrong or how you would limit it.

cards.title: "Fine. Is it worth it?"
body: Say you named the trade-offs. Your spreadsheet has 14 numbers. You have time for one sentence.

image.label: A cluttered spreadsheet next to one highlighted number
image.brief: 왼쪽에는 숫자가 빽빽한 스프레드시트 화면, 오른쪽에는 크게 강조된 숫자 하나('$9,000 / month'). 왼쪽은 흐릿하게, 오른쪽은 선명하게. 실제 소프트웨어 로고 없음.

options.text: Show all 14 numbers on one slide so nothing looks hidden
options.feedback: Thorough, but the CEO has to find the point alone. Most skeptics decide there isn't one.

options.text: "We pay delivery apps about $50,000 a month. Moving 3 in 10 of those orders to our own system saves about $9,000 a month, after software costs."
options.feedback: A starting point, a change and a result. The CEO can check it in their head and still remember it after you leave.

options.text: "The savings could be huge, easily six figures a year."
options.feedback: Maybe true, but with no starting point the CEO can't check it. Big round claims sound like hope.

cards.title: "Send me something. I'll decide Friday."
body: Say you told it with one number. The meeting ends without a yes, but without a no. What do you send?

options.text: The full 20-slide deck, so every detail is there
options.feedback: Nothing is missing, but the point is buried again. The deck works better as an attachment than as the main document.

options.text: One page: the recommendation, the trade-offs, the key number and the decision you need
options.feedback: It repeats what worked in the room, in two minutes of reading. The CEO can also forward it to the finance lead without you there.

options.text: A short email: "Thanks for your time! Let me know."
options.feedback: Polite, but the CEO must rebuild your case from memory. By Friday, most of what you said is gone.

cards.title: The CEO said yes to the test.
body: On Friday, the CEO approved the 90-day test in three restaurants. The idea wasn't new. What changed was how each answer landed.

A skeptic usually isn't asking, "Is this a good idea?" They're asking, **"Can I trust this person with the risk?"** Every move you made answered that question: a clear ask, costs you named yourself, a number they could check, and a page they could reread.

image.label: The CEO signing a one-page memo
image.brief: CEO가 책상에서 종이 한 장에 서명하는 장면. 옆에 세 개 매장 위치가 표시된 작은 지도와 '90 days' 메모. 따뜻한 톤. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Good delivery can't rescue a weak idea.
body: These moves make a sound case easy to judge. They don't make a weak case strong. If the CEO's objection reveals a real flaw, say so and rework the plan. Winning the meeting and being wrong is worse than losing it.
Skepticism also has a cause. Before you pitch, find out why past projects failed. It often tells you which objection is coming.
cards.softwareNote: The same pattern holds when a software founder pitches a board: lead with the ask, name the risks, show one number such as monthly churn before and after, and follow up with a short written memo.

cards.title: Answer the question a skeptic is really asking.
body: Four moments, four ideas from this unit:
list: **The pushback:** present the trade-offs before they're found
**The numbers:** tell the story with one number
cards.callout: **Try it today:** before your next pitch, write the one sentence you'll open with and the biggest downside you'll name yourself.
